[Operator Instructions] And as a reminder, today's conference is being recorded. And now I would like to turn the call over to your host, Jeff Evanson. Jeffrey K. Evanson Former Vice President of Investor Relations Thank you, John, and good afternoon, everyone, and our welcome as well to our Q&A webcast. I'm joined today by Elon Musk, Tesla's Chairman and CEO; and Deepak Ahuja, Tesla's Chief Financial Officer. We announced the financial results for our third quarter shortly after the close of trading today. The shareholder letter, financial results and webcast of this Q&A session are all available at our Investor Relations website at ir.teslamotors.com. A replay of this webcast will be available at the same site later today. Please note that certain financial measures that we use on the call, such as revenue and income, are expressed on a non-GAAP basis and have been adjusted to exclude the effects of lease accounting on Model S sales and changes related to stock-based compensation and noncash interest expense. Our GAAP results and reconciliations of non-GAAP to GAAP measures can be found in our earnings press release. During the course of this call, we may discuss our business outlook and make forward-looking statements. Such statements are predictions based on management's expectations as of today. Actual events or results could differ materially due to a number of risks and uncertainties, including those mentioned in our most recently filed 10-Q with the SEC. And now, John, why don't you give the instructions for asking a question, and then we'll turn it right on to our first question. TESLA, INC. All Rights reserved. spglobal.com/marketintelligence 5 Question and Answer Operator [Operator Instructions] And we'll take our first question from Jamie Albertine from Stifel. James Joseph Albertine Stifel, Nicolaus & Company, Incorporated, Research Division The first question I had was going back to some comments you had made on the last quarterly conference call around gross margin visibility. I think, if I heard it correctly, you basically said you had a pretty good feel where the fourth quarter was going to be about a month before the fourth quarter happened. So given the sequential gross margin expansion that we saw in the third quarter, what update are you able to give us for the fourth quarter at this point? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Sure. So we expect to track to 25% gross margin in the fourth quarter, excluding ZEV credits, so excluding the zero emission vehicle credit. Yes, I feel pretty confident about that outcome, unless there's some force majeure event. And also, we're roughly halfway through the fourth quarter, so I think that's -- almost half. Halfway through. So I think that's pretty secure. And then we'll probably deliver more cars. One thing that I hope was clear in the shareholder letter, or maybe it wasn't, is that we really are production-constrained, not demand-constrained. So we're working hard to address the production constraints and then improve the effective deliveries. Because the thing that people still don't quite get is that we're different in that fundamental way from other car companies, and it doesn't make sense for us to do things to amplify demand if we can't meet that demand with production. So what we spend our time doing here with the management team is trying to figure out how do we ramp up production faster and obviously maintain good quality and keep improving the product. And yes, that's where we -- we expect to alleviate a lot of those production constraints next year. James Joseph Albertine Stifel, Nicolaus & Company, Incorporated, Research Division That's great. As a quick follow-up maybe, given some of the announcements that you'd made intra- quarter and then you alluded to in your shareholders' letter, what does your sort of feel on the current assembly line capacity, as it stands today, look like today versus maybe how you felt 3 months ago? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect The main constraint on our production is really -- is the sales. And I think I've mentioned that before in talks, and I think I alluded to that on the prior earnings call. So we're addressing the cell supply constraint and any sort of constraints that are -- again, non-cell constraints that exist. But really, the critical thing is the cell production constraints. Actually, we announced the deal recently with Panasonic, which has very much increased volume, and we're -- when we think about the constraint on growth, that's the biggest item, and that gets the most of our attention. And like I said, I think we'll see some relief on that constraint next year. Operator We'll take our next question coming from Craig Irwin from Wedbush Securities. Craig Edward Irwin Wedbush Securities Inc., Research Division So, Elon, I wanted to ask a more philosophical question of [ph] you. We're hearing from different sources that the cost of your Model S drivetrain is more or less at parity with some of the conventional ice vehicles out there, some of the premium vehicles in the market. Now with the visibility on battery cost coming TESLA, INC. FQ3 2013 EARNINGS CALL | NOV 05, 2013 Copyright © 2019 S&P Global Market Intelligence, a division of S&P Global Inc. All Rights reserved. spglobal.com/marketintelligence 6 down fairly significantly over the next few years, when you look at the Gen3 vehicle, would you still want to price that at a premium versus comparable vehicles, where you would basically be benefiting from the ROI that you offer to the customer, basically less expensive gas in the tank considering they're not using petroleum, they'll be using clean electricity? Or would you consider pricing that more or less at parity or possibly at a discount versus the conventional competition? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect So I think what it stood for is that we wanted to try to price the Gen3 vehicle at around the $35,000 price point. And when you consider the savings from gasoline, [indiscernible] to consider gasoline to be at that point -- I mean, it's effectively like buying a gasoline car in the U.S. for maybe $28,000 or a gasoline car in Europe for maybe $22,000. So that makes it pretty competitive. And as we -- over time, we're going to get better and better at our lease offerings with lower interest rates and just better access to capital with a track record and more visibility into residual values. I mean, I think our residual values can be very good. But therefore, to get the lowest cost of capital, you have to kind of prove that. And I think long term, just like with SolarCity, I see leasing as being, overwhelmingly, the path to go for electric cars because it just brings the cost of transportation -- it makes it immediate. Because if you have the lease and you look at your -- the amount you are paying for a month, you might, you might -- plus the amount you might pay for electricity versus your gasoline car lease plus gasoline costs, and I think gasoline cars also really inherently require more maintenance, so there's that as well, and with a lease, you don't have to worry about like capturing a savings over a certain period of time or worry about the battery life or anything like that. You just experience those savings immediately. So long term, I see leasing as being the main way that people buy our car. And then it's going to -- I think it's going to seem like a very compelling value proposition. Craig Edward Irwin Wedbush Securities Inc., Research Division Great. Then this second question I wanted to ask was about the priorities for R&D investment in '14 and, I guess, over the intermediate term. Can you discuss the breadth of projects that you will be looking to fund and whether or not this is an acceleration from your prior plans? Or if this is consistent with what you had been thinking previously? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect I think it's more or less consistent. The thing that we're looking to be doing in '14 is expanding Model S deliveries worldwide, particularly into Asia and then more broadly into Europe and as well as other parts of the world. So it's kind of international expansion and volume production expansion with Model S and then development of the Model X. It's just refining all of that, getting the tooling in place and building out a really high-volume production line, kind of next-generation production line for the S and the X. Next year, we'll also be doing the design work, the sort of styling, essentially, of the third generation vehicle, because we'll be done with the Model X styling essentially in -- the fine brush strokes in the next few months. So next year is going to be about really getting that design of the third generation car done. But then it's going to take us a while to build out the capacity for that third generation vehicle, and we're going to have to sort out [ph] selling battery pack capacity because we're -- ultimately, we need -- if we were to produce 500,000 vehicles a year from the former NUMMI plant, then we need cell capacity that's commensurate with that, which is maybe bigger than all the lithium-ion production in the world today, or at least on par with it. Craig Edward Irwin Wedbush Securities Inc., Research Division Excellent. And then my last question, if I can squeeze it in, the Panasonic agreement, 1.8 billion cells over 4 years, my back -- back of the envelope math is if we assume 85 kilowatt hour Model Ss, probably one of the larger batteries of what you're going to produce over the next few years, a thing like 250,000 cars, there's obviously been a lot of press coverage of your discussions and qualification of Samsung, so TESLA, INC. All Rights reserved. spglobal.com/marketintelligence 7 I'm going to guess there's incremental demand on top of that, that you anticipate to have. Can you sort of shape that for us, how you potentially see the ramp and how you would look for the stagger in these supply agreements to work? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Well, certainly, I -- people shouldn't look at the x number of sales over 4 years. I assume that, that's the hard number of cars that we'll make. I think we'll make, towards the back end of that, a lot more cars. And so there will need to be other agreements with some combination of Panasonic, maybe with others. Panasonic is obviously our primary partner, but when it comes to the high volume, third generation vehicle, it's clear that there's going to need to be incremental production capacity created that doesn't exist in the world today. So we're in the process of figuring that out, and there's going to need to be some kind of giga factory built. Operator And our next question comes from Dan Galves from Deutsche Bank. Daniel V. Galves Deutsche Bank AG, Research Division Wanted to ask about kind of the current level of demand. We've seen this -- apparently, the order to delivery time has expanded over the last couple of months, customer deposit account went up quite a bit in Q3 and you kind of confirmed that you're seeing demand increases. Can you quantify that at all in terms of how many orders you took in Q3 versus Q2? Or just kind of a more order of magnitude? Is the U.S. demand continuing to increase? Where does Europe stand compared to where you were, let's say, at the same point in kind of the U.S. launch process? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Well, U.S. demand or North American demand has continued to increase. We've actually had to stop North American demand in order to feed Europe. So we've had European customers that have been waiting for a long time, so we've had to constrain deliveries to North America in order to get people their cars. They've been waiting, in some cases, 2 or 3 years. I mean, I think we could sustain 20,000 cars a year in North America and maybe more than that. But it doesn't make sense for us to try to amplify demand if we aren't able to deliver to that demand. It just makes people unhappy. So where we are in Europe is -- we're still up the early stages. I mean, we're kind of in Europe where we were in the U.S. maybe in January or February of this year. So European demand is -- well, [indiscernible] demand, it's like -- it's on the order of maybe 10,000 units a year. But again, it doesn't make sense for us to try to drive that demand higher if we aren't able to meet it. We want to make sure that we're laying the groundwork for future demand increase. And I think we could get demand in kind of the greater Europe to be similar to that of North America. It seems like that's -- that seems pretty achievable to me. Daniel V. Galves Deutsche Bank AG, Research Division Okay, great. And I just wanted to ask about kind of the production ramp. I mean, you said that kind of cell capacity or cell flow is kind of the biggest constraint right now. You seem to be addressing that. Where do you see kind of production per week going over the next few quarters? And also, I would expect you'd continue to deliver significantly less than you produce as you continue to have more and more vehicles on ships at the end of the quarter versus the previous quarter. Is that correct? Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes. I mean, as deliveries to Europe increase, then we have -- we necessarily have more inventory in transit. And then as we start adding Asia in there, we've got even more in transit. Then we'll probably have 60%-plus of our sales going outside the U.S. and to Europe and Asia and potentially across the world TESLA, INC. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes. So we have all the potential approvals from the Chinese regulatory authorities to ship the car, and we expect to probably ship out -- put our first cars on a boat in January. And so they'll be arriving in February if things go according to plan. We'll still be somewhat production constrained, so it doesn't make sense for us to expand the scope of our sales territories too fast if we're production constrained, because it just amplifies the set of problems we have to deal with. But we do want to get some cars to China in first quarter and kind of lay the groundwork in terms of service centers, superchargers and so forth for, hopefully, significant growth in the rest of the year in China. Deepak Ahuja Former Chief Financial Officer And despite the soft initial opening, we are seeing pretty good initial demand in China. It's remarkable [indiscernible] ... Elon R. Musk Co-Founder, CEO, Director & Product Architect Yes. We're not really even trying. Like we're really -- we're soft as -- when I say soft, we really mean soft. Andrea Susan James Dougherty & Company LLC, Research Division And then just one final. The raw materials, though, that seems -- is that -- correct to assume that not an issue, raw material supply? Lithium is like maybe 1% of the cell math-ish, maybe 2%. Sorry, 2/3 of the pack mass [ph] , maybe, or 1/3 of the pack mass [ph] , I should say, 2% of the cell math.
